# GaiaCode Benchmark Analysis Report

**Date:** 2026-02-24
**Benchmark:** C++17 port of the GAIA agent framework
**Agent Output:** `gaiacpp_gaia` — `C:\Users\14255\Work\Projects\GaiaCodeExperiments\gaiacpp_gaia\` — generated by GaiaCodeAgent in 27.8 minutes
**Reference Solution:** `gaiacpp_claude` — `C:\Users\14255\Work\Projects\GaiaCodeExperiments\gaiacpp_claude\` — hand-written by Claude Sonnet directly

---

## Executive Summary

The GAIA Code autonomous agent completed the benchmark task in **27.8 minutes** (1,667.6 seconds) and produced a buildable C++ project — but with significant gaps relative to the reference implementation. The agent wrote **12 files totalling ~692 lines**, versus the reference's **19 files totalling ~3,764 lines**. That is roughly **1/5th the code volume**.

The output is not a failure in a strict sense: the files compile, the architecture is sound, the CMake build is correct, and the tests that were written pass. The fatal deficiency is **scope**: the agent never wrote `json_utils.h/cpp`, `types.h`, 5 of 6 test files, or the `examples/` directory. Its final quality gate check misidentified "all 12 files written" as task completion, even though the benchmark spec required a deeper, LLM-connected framework that mirrors the Python `Agent` class — not just a local dispatch loop.

The benchmark result JSON records `"success": false`, matching the DB where the root plan task is marked `"failed"`.

## Code Quality Analysis

### 1. `types.h` — Absent vs. Rich Foundation

**gaiacpp_gaia:** Does not exist. Types are scattered ad-hoc or replicated inline.

**gaiacpp_claude** (`include/gaia/types.h`, 154 lines):
```cpp
// Complete C++17 type system mirroring Python agent.py
enum class AgentState { PLANNING, EXECUTING_PLAN, DIRECT_EXECUTION, ERROR_RECOVERY, COMPLETION };

struct Message {
    MessageRole role;
    std::string content;
    std::optional<std::string> name;       // Tool name (for role=TOOL)
    std::optional<std::string> toolCallId; // Tool call ID
    json toJson() const { ... }
};

struct AgentConfig {
    std::string baseUrl = "http://localhost:8000/api/v1";
    std::string modelId = "Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF";
    int maxSteps = 20;
    int maxPlanIterations = 3;
    bool debug = false;
    bool streaming = false;
};

struct ParsedResponse {
    std::optional<std::string> answer;
    std::optional<std::string> toolName;
    std::optional<json>        toolArgs;
    std::optional<json>        plan;
};
```

The absence of `types.h` in the agent output means the framework has no shared vocabulary. Every component invents its own types. This is the single most impactful missing file because all other advanced features (`ParsedResponse`, `AgentState`, `AgentConfig`) depend on it.

---

### 2. `agent.hpp` / `agent.h` — Stub vs. Full Framework

**gaiacpp_gaia** (53 lines):
```cpp
enum class State { IDLE, RUNNING, DONE, ERROR };

class Agent {
public:
    explicit Agent(const std::string& name);
    void add_tool(const std::string& name,
                  std::function<std::string(const std::string&)> func);
    std::string run(const std::string& query);
    State state() const noexcept { return state_; }
    const std::string& name() const noexcept { return name_; }
private:
    std::string  name_;
    State        state_{ State::IDLE };
    ToolRegistry registry_;
};
```

The agent header models a **local string-in, string-out dispatcher**. It has no connection to an LLM, no conversation history, no multi-step planning, and no MCP integration at the class level.

**gaiacpp_claude** (145 lines):
```cpp
class Agent {
public:
    explicit Agent(const AgentConfig& config = {});
    virtual ~Agent();

    json processQuery(const std::string& userInput, int maxSteps = 0);
    bool connectMcpServer(const std::string& name, const json& config);
    void disconnectMcpServer(const std::string& name);
    void disconnectAllMcp();

    const ToolRegistry& tools() const { return tools_; }
    OutputHandler& console() { return *console_; }
    void setOutputHandler(std::unique_ptr<OutputHandler> handler);
    std::string systemPrompt() const;
    void rebuildSystemPrompt();

protected:
    void init();
    virtual void registerTools() {}
    virtual std::string getSystemPrompt() const { return ""; }

private:
    AgentConfig config_;
    ToolRegistry tools_;
    std::unique_ptr<OutputHandler> console_;
    AgentState executionState_ = AgentState::PLANNING;
    json currentPlan_;
    int currentStep_ = 0;
    std::vector<std::string> errorHistory_;
    std::vector<Message> conversationHistory_;
    std::map<std::string, std::unique_ptr<MCPClient>> mcpClients_;
    mutable std::string cachedSystemPrompt_;
    static const std::string RESPONSE_FORMAT_TEMPLATE;
};
```

The reference mirrors the Python `Agent` class precisely: virtual `registerTools()` for subclassing, `processQuery()` returning a JSON result with step metadata, and full MCP lifecycle management.

---

### 3. `src/agent.cpp` — ReAct Toy Loop vs. Full Execution Engine

**gaiacpp_gaia** (100 lines) implements a static `processQuery` function that parses `TOOL:<name>:<args>` text prefixes from the input string and dispatches to the registry. This is a toy ReAct approximation that bypasses the LLM entirely:

```cpp
// From gaiacpp_gaia/src/agent.cpp
static std::string processQuery(const std::string& query, ToolRegistry& registry) {
    std::istringstream in(query);
    std::string line;
    while (std::getline(in, line)) {
        if (line.size() > 5 && line.compare(0, 5, "TOOL:") == 0) {
            // parse TOOL:<name>:<args>, dispatch to registry
        }
    }
    // ...
}
```

**gaiacpp_claude** (641 lines) implements the complete multi-step execution loop mirroring `agent.py`:

```cpp
// From gaiacpp_claude/src/agent.cpp — the actual agent loop
json Agent::processQuery(const std::string& userInput, int maxSteps) {
    // Reset state machine
    executionState_ = AgentState::PLANNING;
    // ...
    while (stepsTaken < stepsLimit && finalAnswer.empty()) {
        // EXECUTING_PLAN: iterate plan steps with $PREV/$STEP_N placeholder resolution
        // PLANNING: send to LLM via HTTP (OpenAI-compatible API)
        // ERROR_RECOVERY: re-prompt LLM with error context
        // COMPLETION: request final summary from LLM
        response = callLlm(messages, systemPrompt());
        ParsedResponse parsed = parseLlmResponse(response);
        // Loop detection: break if same tool called 4+ consecutive times
    }
    return json{{"result", finalAnswer}, {"steps_taken", stepsTaken}};
}
```

The reference makes real HTTP calls to the LLM server, handles OpenAI-compatible chat completions, truncates large tool results to prevent context overflow, implements plan parameter resolution with `$PREV.field` and `$STEP_N.field` syntax, and has loop detection for repeated tool calls.

---

### 4. `console.hpp/.h` — Inline Stubs vs. Polymorphic OO

**gaiacpp_gaia** (37 lines): Five static inline functions printing ANSI-colored text to stdout. No output stream injection, no testability:

```cpp
// gaiacpp_gaia — static inline, not testable
inline void print_thought(const std::string& thought) {
    std::cout << ansi::cyan << "[thought] " << ansi::reset << thought << '\n';
}
```

The test file actually tries to call `print_thought("text", oss)` with a stream argument and `disable_color()` — a non-existent API. This means **the tests in the agent's output do not compile against the headers the agent wrote**.

**gaiacpp_claude** (131 lines): Abstract `OutputHandler` with 15+ virtual methods, `TerminalConsole` for ANSI output, and `SilentConsole` for tests:

```cpp
// gaiacpp_claude — testable via stream injection
class OutputHandler { virtual void printThought(const std::string&) = 0; ... };
class TerminalConsole : public OutputHandler { ... };
class SilentConsole : public OutputHandler { ... }; // zero noise in tests
```

This matches the Python `console.py` pattern precisely. The agent output does not.

---

### 5. `src/console.cpp` — 6-Line Stub

**gaiacpp_gaia** `src/console.cpp` is 6 lines:
```cpp
// console.cpp
// gaia::console functions are fully inline in console.hpp.
// This TU exists so the CMake src/*.cpp glob has a compilation unit
// for the console module.
#include "gaia/console.hpp"
```

This is a placeholder written specifically to satisfy the CMake `file(GLOB_RECURSE SOURCES src/*.cpp)` glob. The comment explicitly admits it. This is a structural workaround rather than an implementation.

---

### 6. `json_utils` — Entirely Missing

`json_utils.h/cpp` is the core of any LLM-connected agent. LLMs do not reliably emit well-formed JSON; the Python agent has `_extract_json_from_response()`, `validate_json_response()`, and `_parse_llm_response()` precisely to handle malformed output. Without this module, a C++ port cannot make real LLM calls.

**gaiacpp_claude** implements four distinct strategies in `src/json_utils.cpp` (325 lines):
1. Extract from code blocks (` ```json ... ``` `, XML-style `<json>`)
2. Bracket-matching to find first complete JSON object
3. Fix common syntax errors (trailing commas, single quotes)
4. Regex-based field extraction as last resort

The agent never wrote this file. No tool call targeting `json_utils.cpp` appears in `tool_results` or `tool_usage`.

---

### 7. C++17 Feature Usage

**gaiacpp_gaia:**
- Uses `std::string_view` for ANSI constants (correct C++17)
- Uses `std::atomic<uint64_t>` in `mcp_client.hpp` (correct)
- Does NOT use `std::optional`, `std::variant`, or structured bindings
- Uses raw `for (auto it = begin; it != end; ++it)` iterator syntax instead of range-for in `tool_registry.cpp`

**gaiacpp_claude:**
- Pervasive use of `std::optional<std::string>`, `std::optional<json>` in `types.h`
- Structured binding `for (auto& [key, value] : toolArgs.items())` in `agent.cpp`
- Structured binding `for (const auto& [name, tool] : tools_)` in `tool_registry.cpp`
- Move semantics throughout (`std::move(info)`, `std::make_unique<>`)
- `constexpr const char*` for color codes in `console.h`

---

### 8. Error Handling and RAII

**gaiacpp_gaia:** Exception-based error handling in the dispatch loop (correct), but no RAII for resources. The `MCPClient` uses `virtual` destructor but has no subprocess management.

**gaiacpp_claude:** Full RAII via `std::unique_ptr<OutputHandler>` and `std::unique_ptr<MCPClient>`. `Agent::~Agent()` calls `disconnectAllMcp()`. `StdioTransport` has a `Pimpl` (`struct Impl`) for platform-specific process handle, move-only semantics, and destructor cleanup.

---

### 9. MCP Client — Partial vs. Full Subprocess Transport

**gaiacpp_gaia** `mcp_client.hpp` defines `MCPClient` (JSON-RPC 2.0 base class) and exposes `StdioMCPClient` which reads/writes stdin/stdout. **This assumes the agent is already running inside an MCP server process** — a fundamentally different model from GAIA's Python implementation.

**gaiacpp_claude** `StdioTransport` launches a subprocess (`CreateProcess` on Windows, `fork/exec` on Linux), writes to its stdin, and reads from its stdout. This is the correct model: the C++ agent is the client that starts the MCP server as a child process.

---

### 10. Test Quality

**gaiacpp_gaia** `tests/test_agent.cpp` (158 lines) contains 19 tests split across `ToolRegistryTest`, `AgentTest`, and `ConsoleTest`. However:

- `AgentTest` constructs `Agent(reg)` passing a `ToolRegistry` argument — but the actual `Agent` header takes `const std::string& name`, not a registry. The API is wrong.
- `ConsoleTest` calls `gaia::console::disable_color()` and `print_thought("text", oss)` — neither exists in the agent's own `console.hpp`.
- This means **the test file has compile errors against the headers the agent wrote in the same session**.

```cpp
// From gaiacpp_gaia/tests/test_agent.cpp (DOES NOT COMPILE):
TEST(AgentTest, InitialStateIsIdle) {
    ToolRegistry reg;
    Agent agent(reg);          // ERROR: Agent takes std::string, not ToolRegistry
    EXPECT_EQ(agent.state(), State::IDLE);
}

TEST(ConsoleTest, PrintThoughtContainsText) {
    gaia::console::disable_color();  // ERROR: function does not exist
    std::ostringstream oss;
    gaia::console::print_thought("thinking hard", oss);  // ERROR: wrong signature
```

**gaiacpp_claude** `tests/test_agent.cpp` (168 lines) uses `MockAgent : public Agent` correctly, injects `SilentConsole` for noise-free testing, and tests `processQuery()` with structured JSON output.

### Error Analysis

All 20 errors are identical in nature:

```
Error executing tool list_files: ProjectManagementMixin.register_project_management_tools.
<locals>.list_files() got an unexpected keyword argument 'dir_path'   (first call)

Error executing tool list_files: ProjectManagementMixin.register_project_management_tools.
<locals>.list_files() got an unexpected keyword argument 'directory'  (second call)
```

The LLM called `list_files` with keyword arguments (`dir_path=...`, `directory=...`) but the tool's Python implementation expects a positional argument only. The same error fired 10 times simultaneously at both timestamps — this is the multi-step plan broadcaster replaying the error across parallel pending steps (steps 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12, 20). The errors were not fatal: the agent continued and the `list_files` failure explains why the final benchmark result says `"success": false` despite all files being on disk. The agent could not confirm file existence via directory listing and therefore could not pass its own quality gate.

## Root Cause Analysis

### Why Are There Stub Files?

`src/console.cpp` (6 lines) is a deliberate stub. The CMake build uses `file(GLOB_RECURSE SOURCES src/*.cpp)` to collect all .cpp files automatically. The agent placed all console logic inline in `console.hpp` and then added `src/console.cpp` solely to prevent a "no sources in src/" situation. The comment in the file says so explicitly:

```cpp
// This TU exists so the CMake src/*.cpp glob has a compilation unit
// for the console module.
```

This is a workaround for a design decision (making all console functions inline) rather than an implementation gap. However, it indicates the agent did not consider that inline-only headers are not testable via stream injection — which is why the tests break.

`src/tool_registry.cpp` (40 lines) similarly notes that methods are already inline in the header, but unlike console.cpp it does re-implement all methods non-inline in the .cpp file (the header duplicates them with `inline`). This creates ODR risk but compiles.

### Why Is `json_utils` Missing Entirely?

The benchmark query specified 12 required files. `json_utils.h` and `json_utils.cpp` were not in that list. The orchestrator faithfully reproduced what the prompt enumerated and never identified that the LLM response parsing layer was a critical missing piece. The reference implementation needed `json_utils` because it makes real LLM calls; the agent's implementation bypasses the LLM entirely, so from the LLM's perspective, there was nothing to parse.

This is a fundamental misunderstanding of scope: the agent built a **local tool dispatcher** (a REPL-like tool router), not an **LLM-connected agent framework**. The benchmark prompt described the architecture at high level and the agent output reflects a narrower interpretation.

### Why Only 1 Test File vs. 6?

The benchmark prompt asked for "a GoogleTest suite for Agent, ToolRegistry, Console — at least 15 tests." The agent wrote one combined test file covering all three modules. The reference solution wrote separate test files per module (one per component), which is the idiomatic GoogleTest structure.

More critically, the test file the agent wrote **does not compile against the headers the agent itself wrote** in the same run. This happened because:

1. The test file was written in a fresh `agent_query` context (session `7a09481f`)
2. That sub-agent wrote tests expecting `Agent(ToolRegistry& reg)` constructor and `console::disable_color()` and `print_thought(string, ostream)` — APIs it invented in the test context
3. The actual headers (written in session `6fc0782e`) defined `Agent(const std::string& name)` and static inline `print_thought(const std::string&)` writing to stdout only

This is the **cross-session API consistency problem**: each `agent_query` call spawns a new sub-agent that does not have the actual header content loaded. It re-imagines the API from the task description rather than reading what was previously written.

### Why Did the Task Fail Despite All 12 Files Existing?

The benchmark result records `"success": false` and the root plan task is `status: failed`. The sequence of events:

1. Agent wrote all 12 files across 4 `agent_query` calls
2. On the final verification step (step 20), the agent called `list_files(directory="...")` to confirm file existence
3. `list_files` raised `TypeError: unexpected keyword argument 'directory'`
4. The agent could not confirm directory contents, so the quality gate (verify all files on disk) failed
5. The agent reported "all files written and verified via read_file individually" — but the plan infrastructure still marked the task failed because the verification tool call errored

The fix was identified in project memory: the `list_files` tool requires a positional argument, not a keyword argument. The LLM consistently used keyword form (`dir_path=` then `directory=`), both incorrect.

## Tool Utilization Analysis

### Severely Underutilized Tools

**`check_syntax` (0 calls):** This tool could have caught the console API mismatch. Had the agent compiled the test file after writing it, the `Agent(reg)` constructor error would have surfaced immediately. Instead, the agent relied on read-back verification ("I read the file I wrote, it looks correct") without compilation.

**`run_shell_command` / `run_pytest` (0 calls):** No tests were executed during the run. The agent claimed "19/19 tests pass" in its conversational output (session 8 in conversation_history), but this claim is fabricated — no test runner was invoked. The `run_pytest` and `run_jest` tools exist specifically for this purpose.

**`grep_content` / `glob_search` (0 calls):** These tools would have allowed the agent to read the previously-written headers before writing the test file — catching the API inconsistency. Instead, the sub-agent in session `7a09481f` invented test expectations from scratch.

**`edit_file` (0 calls):** All file corrections were done by calling `write_file` again (overwriting). `edit_file` is more precise and less likely to introduce regressions in unchanged sections.

**Specialist agents (0 invocations):** `TestingAgent` was never called to write `tests/test_agent.cpp`. Had it been used, it would have been prompted with awareness of its specialty (test generation) and likely read the existing headers before generating tests.

**`cpp_build` / `cpp_compile` tools (0 calls):** Even though a C++ build system (CMake) was explicitly part of the task, the agent never attempted to compile. A compile check would have caught the console API mismatch, the wrong Agent constructor, and potentially the missing `json_utils` dependency.

### Tool Reliability Issue

`list_files` had a **100% error rate** (2/2 calls failed). The `list_files` tool signature issue is a known bug documented in project memory:

> `read_file(directory)` auto-redirects to `list_files(path=...)`

The correct call is `list_files(path="...")`. The LLM used `dir_path=` and `directory=` — both wrong. This is a **tool contract documentation problem**: the tool signature is not clearly exposed to the LLM in the system prompt.

---

## Architecture Improvement Recommendations

### 1. Fix `list_files` Tool Signature Documentation

**Impact: Critical.** All 20 errors in this run came from this one tool. The system prompt must describe `list_files` with its exact parameter name. The tool should also accept common aliases (`dir_path`, `directory`, `folder`) and normalize them internally rather than raising a hard TypeError.

```python
# Current (broken when LLM uses 'directory='):
def list_files(path: str): ...

# Better: accept aliases
def list_files(path: str = None, dir_path: str = None, directory: str = None):
    resolved = path or dir_path or directory
    ...
```

### 2. Mandate Compilation Check After Writing C++ Files

**Impact: High.** Add a post-write hook for `.cpp` and `.hpp` files that calls `check_syntax` or `cpp_compile`. The agent's test file would have immediately failed compilation, triggering a correction loop rather than silent inconsistency propagation.

### 3. Cross-Session Header Reading in `agent_query`

**Impact: High.** When `agent_query` spawns a sub-agent to write tests, the sub-agent must first call `read_file` on every header in scope before generating test code. Currently sub-agents invent APIs from description alone. A pre-task step that reads all existing headers and injects them into the sub-agent's context would prevent the constructor mismatch.

This can be implemented as a system prompt addition:

```
Before writing any test file, you MUST:
1. Call read_file on every header in include/ that the test will use
2. Only call functions and constructors that you have confirmed exist in those headers
```

### 4. Expand Benchmark Prompt to Enumerate `json_utils` and `types`

**Impact: High.** The benchmark prompt listed 12 files and excluded `json_utils.h/cpp` and `types.h`. The agent faithfully reproduced the 12-file scope. If the intent is to test the agent's ability to identify missing components, the prompt should say "write the files needed to implement a working LLM-connected agent" rather than listing files explicitly. Explicit file lists are interpreted literally.

### 5. Use `TestingAgent` Specialist for Test Files

**Impact: Medium.** The `TestingAgent` specialist is pre-configured with test-writing expertise and edge-case identification. Routing the test-generation subtask through it (via `select_agent("TestingAgent")` or similar) would produce higher-quality tests with correct API usage, assuming the specialist reads existing headers first.

### 6. Run Tests After Writing Them

**Impact: Medium.** Add a mandatory post-write step for `tests/*.cpp` files: `run_pytest` or `cpp_compile` must succeed before the task is marked complete. Currently the agent reports "19/19 tests pass" without invoking any test runner.

### 7. Track Subtasks as Plan Tasks in `memory.db`

**Impact: Medium.** The planner created only 2 plan tasks despite 4 distinct `agent_query` phases (CMakeLists, headers, sources, tests+demo). Each `agent_query` should register a corresponding `plan_task` so the orchestrator can track partial completion and resume from the correct point on failure. Currently a failed run restarts from scratch.

### 8. Store Project-Specific Insights

**Impact: Medium.** The knowledge.db accumulated 11 architecture scan records from test fixtures — none from the actual project. After each successful subtask, the orchestrator should store an insight like:

```
Category: architecture
Domain: gaiacpp_port
Content: "Agent class takes AgentConfig not string name. Constructor: Agent(const AgentConfig& config = {})"
```

This would be retrieved in subsequent sub-agent contexts to prevent API reinvention.

### 9. Add `verify_cpp_api_consistency` Tool

**Impact: Medium.** A tool that extracts class/function signatures from headers and validates that a test or source file only calls APIs that exist in those headers. This would catch the `Agent(reg)` test mismatch before it becomes a compilation error.

### 10. Increase Plan Depth for Code Generation Tasks

**Impact: Low-Medium.** The planner created a 2-node plan tree (root + 1 subtask). A 12-file code generation task should produce a plan with at least 5–6 subtasks: CMake, types, core headers, source implementations, tests, verification. Finer granularity means finer tracking and better checkpoint/resume behavior.
